 Brian O’Connell Thu, October 22, 2026 at 5:45 PM EDT 6 min read Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images Rumblings from Washington, D.C., suggest the Trump administration, through the U.S. Department of the Treasury, could start cracking down on defaulted federal student loan borrowers. 
 The USDT is mulling several enforcement options, including hiring more professional debt collectors, garnishing paychecks and withholding some federal benefits, The Washington Sun reported this week.

 The Federal Student Aid estimates nearly $9.3 million student loan borrowers are in default, with 400,000 more added to the default rolls in the quarter ending June 30. 
 "Their outstanding federal student loans total $234 billion, or approximately 14% of the total $1.64 trillion federally managed portfolio as of June 2026," the FSA wrote in a statement. 
 While considering their pivot, The Sun reported that the Trump Administration's priority is to steer borrowers behind on their loan payments to installment plans and leverage the U.S. Treasury's new Defaulted Loans Support Center to "understand the consequences of default and apply online to either rehabilitate or consolidate their loans." The site launched in September. 
 Here's what the government can legally go after 
 Debt experts say the federal government has multiple options when looking to collect on defaulted student loan debt . 
 "A defaulted federal student loan is the one debt that can be collected without a lawsuit," Nick Avila, founder of San Diego-based United Debt Relief, told Moneywise. 
 For instance, the government can order an employer to withhold up to 15% of disposable pay without going to court, take a federal tax refund through the Treasury Offset Program, and offset Social Security benefits, Avila said. 
 It's a little more nuanced when it comes to collecting from Social Security . Hans Goldstein, founder of the Southern California-based Retirement Literacy Foundation, highlighted the challenges the government faces when taking from retirees. 
 If a retired American gets $1,400 a month, 15% is $210, which leaves retirees with $1,190. Meanwhile, another person may get $800 a month, and 15% leaves them with much less, so the government can only skim $50. 
 Story Continues Taxes, on top of that, are another pain point for collectors. 
 "In a given tax year, a borrower may not owe any federal income tax," Dr. Ethan White, co-founder of Los Angeles-based White Sands Tax Services, a family-owned tax preparation company, told Moneywise. "However, a portion or all of the borrower's federal tax refund may still be taken to satisfy a defaulted federal loan, up to the amount owed." 
 Some defaulted borrowers may also rely on a tax refund to pay basic living expenses. 
 "Like a paycheck, a tax refund may be taken through an offset," White said, adding that wage garnishment may take up to 15% of their disposable pay for the week. "However, garnishment must also preserve the equivalent of 30 times the federal minimum hourly wage for the week." 
 That 15% limit could also protect retirees who still work part-time. Marriages may be impacted, too. If defaulted loans are in one spouse's name, a joint refund may still be taken. 
 "However, the spouse who doesn't owe the debt may be able to protect their allocated portion of the refund using Form 8379," White said. 
 Form 8379 may be submitted along with the tax return or may also be submitted after the refund has been taken. 
 "Review this option prior to switching to separate tax filings, which may also incur additional costs," White said.

 Take these steps to protect your financial assets 
 To keep the government's hands out of your pockets, be disciplined and think creatively. Make these strategies a priority when dealing with the federal government. 
 Safeguard your paycheck and benefits 
 Open every notice, because each one has a deadline to request a hearing or review, including for financial hardship , and missing that window is how people lose their options. 
 "Then contact the loan holder before collections start, not after," Avila said. 
 Reprioritize your bills 
 A defaulted student loan also changes how you prioritize your bills. 
 "Most people pay the credit card that calls the most and let the student loan sit," Avila said. "But a credit card company has to sue you before it can touch your wages. A defaulted federal loan doesn't. That moves it up the list." 
 Aim to get out of default 
 Rehabilitation requires nine voluntary, on-time payments within ten months, based on your income. 
 Once it's complete, the default comes off your credit history and the garnishment and offsets stop. 
 "Consolidation is usually faster, but the record of the default stays," Avila said. "For most people who can manage nine payments, rehabilitation is the better long-term path. 
 For retirees and vulnerable households 
 For someone living on Social Security, a 15% offset can be the difference between making rent and not. 
 "That's why getting out of default before collections begin matters so much for older borrowers," Avila said, adding that borrowers with a total and permanent disability should check Studentaid.gov, because they may qualify for a discharge instead of collections. 
 Have a plan for 2027 
 Federal student loan borrowers who are behind on their student loans, or have fallen behind, should log in at Studentaid.gov and confirm the status of every federal loan. 
 "Don't build next year's budget around a tax refund if you're in default," Avila said. "Start rehabilitation now if you can, and keep housing, utilities, and insurance current first. Every path has tradeoffs and results vary, so no one should promise a specific outcome, but the earlier you act, the more choices you keep."
